explain.title: Periods
explain.body: The horizontal rows in the modern periodic table are called periods. There are seven periods in total. Each period represents the completion of a shell. Table (8.1) shows the number of elements and the shell being filled in each period.

explain.title: Groups and families
explain.body: The vertical columns present in the periodic table are called groups. There are eighteen groups. Elements present in a group resemble one another in their chemical properties since they contain the same number of electrons in their outermost shells. A group is also called a family.

explain.title: Group configurations
explain.body: Learn the outermost-shell configurations in Table (8.2). For example, group 1 is ns¹, group 2 is ns², group 17 is ns² np⁵, and group 18 is ns² np⁶.

explain.title: Blocks
explain.body: Elements are classified into s, p, d and f blocks depending upon the type of subshell which is being filled. Groups 1 and 2 are s-block; groups 13 to 18 are p-block; groups 3 to 12 are d-block; and the two rows at the bottom are f-block elements.

explain.title: Lanthanides and actinides
explain.body: The first series of fourteen elements starts after lanthanum and is called lanthanides. The second series starts after actinium and is called actinides. Together these two series are also called rare earths or f-block elements.

mistakes: Mixing up periods and groups: periods are horizontal rows, while groups are vertical columns.
Saying there are eighteen periods; the table has seven periods and eighteen groups.
Naming a block from the group number alone without checking which subshell is being filled.
Forgetting that the period depends on the number of the shell being filled; shorthand such as s²p³ does not itself show that shell number.
Calling the lanthanides and actinides groups instead of two series placed at the bottom of the table.

explain.title: Groups 1 and 2 lose electrons
explain.body: Group 1 elements lose one outermost electron and form positive ions. They are thus known as electropositive metals. explain.title: Groups 16 and 17 gain electrons

explain.body: The reactivity of alkali metals gradually increases down the group. Unlike alkali metals, the reactivity of halogens decreases down the group.

explain.title: Periodicity
explain.body: Periodicity in the properties of the elements occur due to recurrence of similar electronic configuration in the outermost shells. These properties include atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.

explain.title: Atomic radius
explain.body: Atomic radius is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of the two identical bonded atoms. It is expressed in pm(1pm = 10⁻¹²m). Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases because increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer. Down a group, it increases because a new shell is added and inner electrons shield outer electrons.

explain.title: Ionization energy
explain.body: Ionization energy is the amount of energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from the valence shell of an isolated gaseous atom. A smaller atomic radius means stronger attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons, so ionization energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.

explain.title: Electron affinity
explain.body: Electron affinity is the amount of energy change when an electron is added up in the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom. In a group, electron affinity values decrease from top to bottom because atomic size increases and the nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly.

explain.title: Electronegativity
explain.body: Electronegativity of an atom is its electron-attracting ability. It is defined as the force with which an atom attracts the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a bond. It increases from left to right in a period and decreases from top to bottom in a group.

mistakes: Do not confuse atomic radius with the full distance between two identical bonded nuclei; the radius is half that distance.
Do not reverse the general trends: atomic radius increases down a group, while ionization energy and electronegativity decrease down a group.
Do not say that ionization energy is energy released when an electron is added; it is energy required to remove an electron.
When giving a trend across a period, include the reason: increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer.

explain.title: Meaning of metallic character
explain.body: The metallic character is the tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions or cations. An element that loses electrons readily has strong metallic character.

explain.title: Trend down a group
explain.body: Since the ionization energy decreases down the group, the elements have increased ability to lose electrons. For this reason both the metallic character and reactivity increase down the group.

explain.title: Trend across a period
explain.body: As we move from left to right in a period, the nuclear charge increases due to a gradual increase in the number of protons in the nucleus. Owing to this the valence electrons are pulled strongly by the nucleus making it difficult for the atoms to lose electrons. Hence the metallic character decreases in a period from left to right.

explain.title: Reactivity across a period and density
explain.body: The chemical reactivity gradually decreases as we move from left to right in a period through the metals, because losing electrons becomes more difficult. Moving further right towards non-metals, chemical reactivity gradually increases again. Density is mass per unit volume, is expressed in g/cm³, and generally increases down a group.

mistakes: Do not say metallic character increases from left to right; it decreases across a period.
Do not forget the reason for the trend: ionization energy decreases down a group, so losing electrons becomes easier.
Do not treat the reactivity trend across a whole period as a simple continuous decrease; it increases again towards non-metals.
Do not claim density rises at every step in the displayed Group 1 data; describe the trend as general.
Do not confuse electropositive (tendency to lose electrons) with electronegative (tendency to attract electrons).

explain.title: The modern periodic table
explain.body: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. The electronic configuration helps determine an element's period, group and block.

explain.title: Periods, groups and blocks
explain.body: A period is a horizontal row and a group is a vertical column. Elements in a group have related outer-shell arrangements. The four blocks are s, p, d and f.

explain.title: Periodic trends
explain.body: Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases and ionization energy generally increases. Down a group, atomic size and metallic character generally increase.

explain.title: Electrons and bonding
explain.body: Metals tend to lose electrons, while non-metals tend to gain or attract electrons. Ionic bonding generally involves electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal.

explain.title: Using the table
explain.body: The periodic table helps organise elements, compare their properties and predict behaviour from their positions and electron arrangements.

mistakes: Do not confuse atomic number with atomic mass; the modern table is arranged by atomic number.
Do not reverse the across-period trends: atomic radius generally decreases, while ionization energy generally increases.

Do not say oxygen accepts three electrons; it needs two electrons to complete its outer shell.
Write both the comparison and the reason when a question asks for a reason.

notes.title: How the Modern Periodic Table Is Arranged
notes.answer: The modern periodic table arranges elements in increasing atomic number, in periods and groups.
notes.explanation: The modern periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Elements are placed in horizontal periods and vertical groups. Elements in the same group have similar outermost-shell electronic configurations and therefore similar chemical properties.
notes.simple: Think of the periodic table as a chart: elements go from left to right in increasing atomic number, and elements with similar properties are placed in the same vertical column.
examples: Sodium and chlorine are placed in the same period because they are in the same horizontal row.
Elements in one vertical column belong to the same group.
steps: Arrange the elements in ascending order of atomic number.
Read across each horizontal row, called a period.
Read down each vertical column, called a group.
Notice that properties repeat at regular intervals and that elements in a group have similar chemical properties.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the horizontal rows and vertical columns of the periodic table called?
notes.checkAnswer: The horizontal rows are periods, and the vertical columns are groups.

notes.title: Reading periods, groups and blocks
notes.answer: The periodic table has 7 periods and 18 groups. Groups 1 and 2 are s-block; groups 13 to 18 are p-block; groups 3 to 12 are d-block; and the two rows placed at the bottom are f-block elements.
notes.explanation: A period is a horizontal row, and a group is a vertical column. The period tells the number of the shell being filled; the group helps identify how many electrons are in the outermost shell. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
notes.simple: Rows are periods; columns are groups. The row tells which shell is being filled, and the column helps tell the outer-shell electron pattern.
examples: Group 17 has outermost-shell configuration ns² np⁵, so its elements are halogens.
Elements in groups 13 to 18 are p-block elements.
steps: Find whether the element is described by a horizontal row or a vertical column.
Use the period number to identify the shell being filled.
Use the group’s outermost-shell configuration to identify its family and block.

notes.title: Why elements in a group behave alike
notes.explanation: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shells. This is why they tend to form ions in similar ways and show similar chemical properties. Group 1 metals tend to lose one electron; group 2 metals tend to lose two. Group 17 elements tend to gain one electron, while group 16 elements tend to gain two.
notes.simple: Elements in a group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, so they tend to react in similar ways.
examples: Sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺.
Chlorine gains one electron to form Cl⁻.
steps: Find the group of the element.
Use the group’s outer-shell electron pattern.
Decide whether the element tends to lose or gain electrons.
Write the ion with the correct charge.
notes.checkQuestion: What ion does a group 17 element usually form?
notes.checkAnswer: A group 17 element usually gains one electron and forms a 1− anion.

notes.title: Periodic trends in atomic properties
notes.answer: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group; ionization energy and electronegativity generally change in the opposite direction.
notes.explanation: Atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity show regular trends in the periodic table. For example, atomic radius generally decreases across a period, while ionization energy generally increases.
notes.simple: Across a period, atoms generally get smaller and hold their outer electrons more strongly. Down a group, atoms generally get larger.
examples: A carbon–carbon nucleus distance of 154 pm gives a carbon radius of 77 pm.
In Group 1, the atomic radius increases from Li to Cs.
steps: For atomic radius, remember: generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
For ionization energy, remember: generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group.
For the radius of an atom bonded to an identical atom, divide the distance between the two nuclei by 2.
notes.checkQuestion: How does atomic radius generally change from left to right across a period?
notes.checkAnswer: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period.

notes.title: Metallic character and reactivity
notes.answer: Metallic character and reactivity generally increase down a group. Metallic character decreases from left to right in a period.
notes.explanation: Metallic character describes how readily an element loses electrons. In a group, metallic character and reactivity generally increase downwards; across a period, metallic character decreases from left to right.
notes.simple: Metals tend to lose electrons. The easier an atom loses electrons, the more metallic it is.
examples: Potassium is more metallic than sodium because potassium is lower in Group 1.
Sodium is more reactive than magnesium in Period 3, as your textbook explains.
steps: Remember that metallic character means the tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
Down a group, ionization energy decreases, so atoms lose electrons more easily.
Therefore metallic character and reactivity generally increase down a group.
From left to right in a period, the nucleus attracts valence electrons more strongly, so metallic character decreases.
notes.checkQuestion: How does metallic character change down a group?
notes.checkAnswer: Metallic character and reactivity generally increase down a group.

notes.title: How the Periodic Table Organises Elements
notes.answer: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
notes.explanation: The modern periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Their electron arrangements explain their positions and help us understand repeating patterns in their properties.
notes.simple: Elements are arranged by atomic number. Their properties repeat in a pattern because their outer-electron arrangements repeat.
examples: Sodium is in Period 3 and Group 1; it has one electron in its outermost shell.
Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period, while ionization energy generally increases.
steps: Find the element's atomic number.
Use its electron arrangement to identify its period and group.
Use its position to predict trends such as atomic radius and metallic character.

written.text: Why was atomic number chosen to arrange the elements in the periodic table?
modelAnswer: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Atomic number gives the correct order of elements and their properties, unlike atomic mass.

rubric.description: State that the table is arranged by atomic number.
rubric.why: Identifies the basis for the modern arrangement.
rubric.how: Write that elements are arranged in increasing atomic number.

rubric.how: Explain that it gives the correct order and recurring properties.

written.text: What is the significance of the word periodic?
modelAnswer: When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, their properties repeat.
This repetition is the significance of the word periodic.

written.text: Why does the size of a period increase as we move down the periodic table?
modelAnswer: The number of elements in a period is related to the number of electrons that can occupy its shells and subshells.
These available electron positions increase in the lower periods, so period size increases.

rubric.description: Relate the number of elements to electron-shell capacity.
rubric.why: Recognises that period size is linked to electron capacity.

rubric.description: State that lower periods have more available electron capacity.
rubric.why: Explains why lower periods can contain more elements.
rubric.how: Explain that available shells or subshells can accommodate more electrons lower in the table.

written.text: In a group, the elements have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell. Why is it so?
modelAnswer: Elements in the same group have similar electronic configurations in their outermost shells.
Therefore, they have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell.

rubric.description: State that group members share the number of outer electrons.

written.text: Do you expect calcium to be more reactive than sodium? Give the reason of your answer.
modelAnswer: No, calcium is not more reactive than sodium.
Sodium loses its single outermost electron more readily than calcium loses its two outermost electrons.

written.text: Which element has the maximum atomic radius and which element has the minimum atomic radius in third period?
modelAnswer: Sodium has the maximum atomic radius in the third period.
Chlorine has the minimum atomic radius in the third period.

written.text: Why are the most electronegative elements present in sixth and seventh groups?
modelAnswer: The elements of the sixth and seventh groups have six and seven outermost-shell electrons respectively.
They need only two or one electrons to complete their shells and strongly attract electrons.

rubric.why: Explains the strong attraction for bonding electrons.
rubric.how: Explain that this makes them strongly attract electrons.

written.text: The first ionization energy value of magnesium is less than the second one. Give reason.
modelAnswer: After losing its first electron, magnesium forms Mg⁺.
The remaining electrons are attracted more strongly, so more energy is required to remove the second electron.

rubric.why: Explains why the second removal requires more energy.
rubric.how: State that the positive ion holds its remaining electrons more strongly.

written.text: Is it possible for two metals or two non-metals to form an ionic bond?
modelAnswer: Usually, two metals or two non-metals do not form an ionic bond with each other.
An ionic bond is generally formed by transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal.

rubric.why: States the electron-transfer basis of ionic bonding.
rubric.how: Mention electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal.

written.text: Which element has the least value of ionization energy and which element has the highest value of electronegativity?
modelAnswer: Francium has the least value of ionization energy.
Fluorine has the highest value of electronegativity.

written.text: Suppose a new element is discovered. Where would you like to accommodate this element in the periodic table?
modelAnswer: Find the atomic number and electronic configuration of the new element.
Place it in order of increasing atomic number.
Use the number of occupied shells to find its period.
Use its outermost-shell electrons to find its group.

written.text: What is the first element of the periodic table? Will it lose an electron or gain it?
modelAnswer: Hydrogen is the first element of the periodic table.
It has one electron and may lose one electron.
It may also gain one electron to attain a stable arrangement.

written.text: Atomic radii of boron and aluminum are 88 pm and 125 pm respectively. Which element is expected to lose electron or electrons easily?
modelAnswer: Radius of boron = 88 pm; radius of aluminium = 125 pm.
Aluminium has the larger atomic radius.
Its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily.
Therefore, aluminium is expected to lose electron or electrons easily.

rubric.why: Explains the relationship between atomic size and electron loss.
rubric.how: Explain that aluminium's outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and easier to remove.

written.text: How would you find the atomic radius of an atom?
modelAnswer: Measure the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms.
The atomic radius is half of this distance.

written.text: Why is it not possible for oxygen atom to accept three electrons to form O³⁻ ion like nitrogen which can accept electrons to form N³⁻?
modelAnswer: Oxygen has six electrons in its outermost shell and needs two electrons to complete its octet.
If it accepted three electrons, it would have more than an octet in its outermost shell.
Therefore, oxygen does not form O³⁻ like nitrogen forms N³⁻.

written.text: Which information is needed to locate the elements in the periodic table if you do not know its atomic number? Is atomic mass helpful for this purpose?
modelAnswer: The electronic configuration is needed to locate an element if its atomic number is not known.
The number of occupied shells gives its period, and its outermost-shell electrons help identify its group.
Atomic mass is not a reliable basis for the arrangement.
Atomic number gives the correct order of elements.

rubric.why: Distinguishes atomic mass from the reliable modern ordering rule.
rubric.how: State that mass is not reliable for placement and atomic number determines the correct order.

written.text: How many blocks of elements are present in the periodic table? Are these blocks helpful in studying the properties of elements?
modelAnswer: There are four blocks of elements in the periodic table: s, p, d and f.
Yes, these blocks help in studying properties because they show which subshell is being filled.

written.text: Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons. (a) Atomic radius
modelAnswer: Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases from left to right.
The nuclear charge increases, but added electrons enter the same shell.
The stronger attraction between the nucleus and electrons pulls the electrons closer.

written.text: Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons. (b) Ionization energy
modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
Atomic radius decreases and the nuclear attraction on the outer electrons becomes stronger.
Therefore, more energy is needed to remove an outer electron.

rubric.how: State that outer electrons are held more strongly and need more energy to remove.

written.text: Which physical properties of elements may lead us to know what type of bond it will form?
modelAnswer: Electronegativity and ionization energy may help us predict the type of bond an element forms.
They indicate how strongly an atom attracts electrons and how readily it loses them.

modelAnswer: Carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine are four non-metals that exist as solids at normal temperature.

written.text: Arrangement of the elements in the form of a periodic table is a remarkable achievement of chemists. Comment on this statement citing the benefits of this table.
modelAnswer: The periodic table arranges all known elements systematically according to increasing atomic number.
Elements with similar outer electronic configurations are placed in the same groups.
Their positions show periodic repetition and trends in properties.
This arrangement makes it easier to compare elements and predict the properties of an element from its position.

written.text: Both lithium and beryllium show behaviour different from rest of the alkali and alkaline earth metals respectively. Can you think of the possible reasons for this difference?
modelAnswer: Lithium and beryllium have very small atomic and ionic sizes compared with the other members of their groups.
Their small size gives them high charge density and strong attraction for electrons.
Their ionization energies and chemical behaviour therefore differ from those of the other alkali and alkaline earth metals.

written.text: Modern periodic table is the amended form of the earlier table developed by Mandeleev. Elaborate how these two tables are different from each other.
modelAnswer: Mendeleev arranged elements mainly in order of increasing atomic mass and placed elements with similar chemical properties together.
The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number.
The modern arrangement removes inconsistencies that arose when atomic mass was used.
The periodic repetition of properties is explained by the repetition of electronic configurations.
